title: Michael Collins (Irish leader) — Born, Raised, And What Came After

Michael Collins (Irish: Mícheál Ó Coileáin; 16 October 1890 – 22 August 1922) was an Irish revolutionary, soldier and politician who was a leading figure in the early-20th century struggle for Irish independence. Michael Collins (Irish: Mícheál Ó Coileáin; 16 October 1890 – 22 August 1922) was an Irish revolutionary, soldier and politician who was a leading figure in the early-20th century struggle for Irish independence. During the War of Independence he was Director of Intelligence of the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

What Michael Collins (Irish leader) built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. He served in the government of the Irish Republic as the Minister for Home Affairs and later as the Minister for Finance. Collins was Chairman of the Provisional Government of the Irish Free State from January 1922 and commander-in-chief of the National Army from July until he died in an ambush in August 1922, during the Civil War.

By the time Michael Collins (Irish leader) reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Collins was born in Woodfield, County Cork, the youngest of eight children. He moved to London in 1906 to become a clerk in the Post Office Savings Bank at Blythe House.

The rise of Michael Collins (Irish leader) was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. He was a member of the London GAA, through which he became associated with the Irish Republican Brotherhood and the Gaelic League. He was taken prisoner and held in the Frongoch internment camp as a prisoner of war, but he was released in December 1916.

Setbacks came early for Michael Collins (Irish leader), and the response to them is the real story. Collins subsequently rose through the ranks of the Irish Volunteers and Sinn Féin. Sinn Féin's elected members (later known as TDs) formed an Irish parliament, the First Dáil, in January 1919 and declared the independence of the Irish Republic.

The legacy of Michael Collins (Irish leader) outlived the circumstances that produced it. In the ensuing War of Independence, he was Director of Organisation and Adjutant General for the Irish Volunteers, later Director of Intelligence of the IRA. He gained fame as a guerrilla warfare strategist, planning many successful attacks on British forces together with the Squad, such as the "Bloody Sunday" assassinations of key British intelligence agents in November 1920.

Few lives travel as far as that of Michael Collins (Irish leader), and the distance is the point. After the July 1921 ceasefire Collins was one of five plenipotentiaries sent by the Dáil cabinet to negotiate peace terms in London. The resulting Anglo-Irish Treaty, signed in December 1921, would establish the Irish Free State but depended on an oath of allegiance to the Crown.

Collins viewed the treaty as offering "the freedom to achieve freedom", and he helped persuade a majority of the Dáil to ratify the Treaty.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Michael Collins (Irish leader) — in that order. During this time he secretly provided support for an IRA offensive in Northern Ireland. It was soon disrupted by the Irish Civil War, in which Collins was commander-in-chief of the National Army.

The turning point in the life of Michael Collins (Irish leader) looked like a failure at the time. He was shot and killed in an ambush by anti-Treaty forces in August 1922 at Beal na Blatha, County Cork. Collins was born in Woodfield, Sam's Cross, near Rosscarbery, County Cork, on 16 October 1890, the third son and youngest of eight children.

Every biography of Michael Collins (Irish leader) has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. His father, Michael John (1815–1897), was a farmer and amateur mathematician, who had been a member of the Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB). The elder Collins was 60 years old when he married Mary Anne O'Brien, then 23, in 1876.

The education of Michael Collins (Irish leader) happened mostly outside any school. They brought up eight children on a 90-acre (36 ha) farm called Woodfield, which the Collins family had held as tenants for several generations. Michael was six and a half years old when his father died.

What Michael Collins (Irish leader) wanted at the start and what Michael Collins (Irish leader) got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. After the death of her husband, Mary Anne had the small family home rebuilt in 1899–1900 as Woodfield House, a much larger dwelling. Michael Collins (the younger) believed his family were descendants of the Uí Chonaill Gabra.

The defining trait of Michael Collins (Irish leader) was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. He was a bright and precocious child with a fiery temper and a passionate feeling of Irish patriotism. He named a local blacksmith, James Santry, and his headmaster at Lisavaird National School, Denis Lyons, as the first nationalists to personally inspire his "pride of Irishness".

Those who met Michael Collins (Irish leader) at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Lyons was a member of the IRB, while Santry's family had participated in, and forged arms for, the rebellions of 1798, 1848 and 1867. There are a number of anecdotal explanations for the origin of his nickname "the Big Fellow".

The private years of Michael Collins (Irish leader) explain the public decades better than any speech. His family claim that he was called this as a child, as a term of endearment for an adventurous and bold youngest brother. The nickname was established in his teens, long before he became a political or military leader.

The family Michael Collins (Irish leader) came from matters more than the legends admit. During the week he stayed with his sister Margaret Collins-O'Driscoll and her husband Patrick O'Driscoll, while at weekends he returned to the family farm. Patrick O'Driscoll founded the newspaper West Cork People and Collins helped out with general reporting and preparing the issues.

The first real success of Michael Collins (Irish leader) arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Leaving school at fifteen, Collins took the British Civil Service examination in Cork in February 1906 and moved to the home of his sister Hannie in London, where he became a boy clerk in the Post Office Savings Bank at Blythe House. In 1910 he became a messenger at a London firm of stockbrokers, Horne and Company.

The last chapter of Michael Collins (Irish leader) was written long after the fame. While living in London he studied law at King's College London but did not finish. Sam Maguire, a republican from Dunmanway, County Cork, introduced the 19-year-old Collins to the IRB.

The whole life of Michael Collins (Irish leader) reads like a single decision repeated. In 1915 he moved to work in the Guaranty Trust Company of New York where he remained until his return to Ireland the following year joining part-time Craig Gardiner & Co, a firm of accountants in Dawson Street, Dublin. The Irish Volunteers were created in the same year by nationalists in response to the formation of the Ulster Volunteers, an Ulster loyalist body pledged to oppose Home Rule by force.

Between the birth and the legend of Michael Collins (Irish leader) lie the years that actually decide it. An organiser of considerable intelligence, Collins had become highly respected in the IRB. This led to his appointment as financial advisor to Count Plunkett, father of one of the Easter Rising's organisers, Joseph Plunkett.

The reputation of Michael Collins (Irish leader) was built in the middle, not at the edges. Collins took part in preparing arms and drilling troops for the insurrection. When it commenced on Easter Monday 1916, Collins served as Joseph Plunkett's aide-de-camp and bodyguard at the rebellion's headquarters in the General Post Office (GPO) in Dublin.

Somebody like Michael Collins (Irish leader) should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. There he fought alongside Patrick Pearse, James Connolly and other members of the Rising leadership. The Rising was put down after six days, but the insurgents achieved their goal of holding their positions for the minimum time required to justify a claim to independence under international criteria.

The life of Michael Collins (Irish leader) begins far from where the story usually starts. During his screening, Collins was identified as someone who should be selected for further interrogation, harsher treatment or execution. However, he overheard his name being called out so he moved to the other side of the building to identify the speaker.

Michael Collins (Irish leader) was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. In doing so, he joined the group that was later transferred to Frongoch internment camp in Wales after two months captivity in Stafford Gaol. Historian Tim Pat Coogan describes Collins's fortuitous move across the detention room in Richmond Barracks as "one of the luckiest escapes of his life".

To understand where Michael Collins (Irish leader) ended up, start with where Michael Collins (Irish leader) began. Collins first began to emerge as a major figure in the vacuum created by the executions of the 1916 leadership. At Frongoch he was one of the organisers of a programme of protest and non-cooperation with authorities.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Michael Collins (Irish leader) ran through years nobody filmed. The camp proved an excellent opportunity for networking with physical-force republicans from all over the country, of which he became a key organiser. While some celebrated the fact that a rising had happened at all, believing in Pearse's theory of "blood sacrifice" (namely that the deaths of the Rising's leaders would inspire others), Collins railed against the military blunders made.

Each stage of the life of Michael Collins (Irish leader) made the next stage possible. He cited the seizure of indefensible and very vulnerable positions like St Stephen's Green which were impossible to escape from and difficult to supply. Public outcry placed pressure on the British government to end the internment and, in December 1916, the Frongoch prisoners were sent home.

Before his execution, Tom Clarke, first signatory of the 1916 Proclamation and widely considered the Rising's foremost organiser, had designated his wife Kathleen Clarke as the official caretaker of Rising official business, in the event that the leadership did not survive. Clarke had sent out the first post-Rising communiqué to the IRB, declaring the Rising to be only the beginning and directing nationalists to prepare for "the next blow".

Clarke appointed Collins Secretary to the National Aid and Volunteers Dependents Fund and subsequently passed on to him the secret organisational information and contacts which she had held in trust for the independence movement. Collins became one of the leading figures in the post-Rising independence movement spearheaded by Arthur Griffith, editor and publisher of the main nationalist newspaper The United Irishman, which Collins had read avidly as a boy.

By the time Michael Collins (Irish leader) reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Griffith's organisation Sinn Féin was founded in 1905 as an umbrella group to unify all the various factions within the nationalist movement. Under Griffith's policy, Collins and other advocates of the "physical-force" approach to independence gained the cooperation of Sinn Féin, while agreeing to disagree with Griffith's moderate ideas of a dual monarchy solution based on the Hungarian model.

The rise of Michael Collins (Irish leader) was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. The British government and mainstream Irish media had wrongly blamed Sinn Féin for the Rising. This attracted Rising participants to join the organisation in order to exploit the reputation with which such British propaganda had imbued the organisation.

In the 1918 general election Sinn Féin swept the polls throughout much of Ireland, with many seats uncontested, and formed an overwhelming parliamentary majority in Ireland. Like many senior Sinn Féin representatives Collins was elected as an MP (for Cork South) with the right to sit in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom in London.
